question: Compare the effectiveness of voucher systems and tax incentives in reducing undeclared domestic work across EU Member States, highlighting differences in coverage and equity impacts.
reference: Voucher systems are generally more effective in reducing undeclared domestic work across EU Member States, as they simplify formal employment and make it more affordable, leading to a noticeable decline in informal work. They are broader in coverage and tend to be fairer, though they still face challenges in reaching low-income families. In contrast, tax incentives primarily benefit wealthier households and have a limited impact on reducing undeclared work, with a core criticism being their regressive effect on employing households. Both systems have limitations, but voucher systems are more effective in promoting formal employment and equity.
answer:
Evidence on effectiveness is mixed and limited. Voucher systems had generally low reported impact in Austria, Belgium and Greece: Austria’s were scarcely used; a Belgian 2018 study estimated that less than 10% of voucher-paid domestic work had previously been undeclared; and a Greek study indicated undeclared work remained widespread. Sweden’s RUT voucher system was associated with low undeclared-work levels, but the relationship was not substantiated. Tax incentives also varied: they had little effect in Germany, while Spain saw an increase in declared domestic workers after their 2011 introduction, followed by a plateau. The sources do not establish that either instrument is consistently more effective across Member States.

Coverage differs in that voucher systems are described as traceable payment systems specifically targeting domestic work, sometimes combined with tax incentives. Tax incentives are also used in several Member States, but their design and generosity vary; the report notes Portugal’s 5% deduction versus deductions of 20% in most Member States using them. Both approaches may leave gaps: voucher limits can reduce their attractiveness, and incentives may not reach households with little or no income-tax liability.

On equity, tax incentives have a clear regressive impact in some cases: in Germany, higher taxable household income brings greater relief, while low-tax households benefit little or not at all; in Sweden, the highest income decile received 40% of total tax deductions. The pages warn that voucher systems and tax incentives may primarily benefit higher-income households, though they do not provide comparable distributional evidence showing that vouchers are more equitable.

question: Analyze how gender and household status influence underemployment among part-time workers in the EU, and compare the underlying factors driving these patterns.
reference: Underemployment among part-time workers in the EU is influenced by gender and household status. Most underemployed part-time workers are women, middle-aged, domestic-born, and without young children, reflecting their higher likelihood of part-time work and the challenges of combining paid work with family responsibilities. In contrast, underemployment is more common among young, migrant, single part-time workers and those with lower educational attainment. The reasons for underemployment vary, with difficulties in finding a full-time job being the most common reason, but other factors such as the need to combine paid work with care responsibilities or education also play a role. The probability of underemployment is significantly lower among women, older workers, and people living with partners, and higher among younger workers, migrants, and those with lower educational attainment. These differences cannot be fully explained by occupational and sectoral patterns of employment.
answer:
Gender: Women who work part-time are less likely to be underemployed than men. The descriptive figures show underemployment among 18% of women part-time workers, versus more than a quarter of men. The report links women’s lower rates partly to care-related limits on their available paid-work hours: women more often undertake unpaid care, and childcare or long-term-care constraints can prevent them from considering longer hours. Men are less likely to work part-time, but when they do, they are more likely to want longer hours. The report also points to gendered expectations that men are primary earners and women primary caretakers. In the adjusted analysis, women’s probability of underemployment remains at least 8 percentage points lower than men’s.

Household status: Part-time workers living with a partner are less often underemployed than those without a partner—about 15% versus 26%. The report suggests that a two-earner household may be able to maintain sufficient income while one partner works part-time; singles rely more on their own income and may prefer full-time work. The adjusted analysis finds that living with a partner is associated with at least an 8-point lower probability overall. This household effect differs substantially by gender: partnered women are considerably less likely to be underemployed than women without a partner, while having a partner has little effect for men. The report relates this difference to gendered work-and-care expectations and women’s care-related working-time constraints.
